## Grammar

Basic word order is SOV; it has postpositions. In the noun phrase: genitive order varies; noun before the adjective; demonstrative before the noun; numeral before the noun; noun before the relative clause. Overall it is head-final.
It has a definite article before the noun, no indefinite article, no case marking on nouns, split alignment (ergative in some contexts, accusative in others), no grammatical number, a system of noun classes.
Verbs mark past, future and habitual; there are both direct and indirect evidentials. Negation uses a negator after the verb; yes/no questions use intonation alone. Verbs do not agree with their arguments.
Other features: pronouns can be dropped; alienable and inalienable possession told apart; serial verbs; verb reduplication; a copula; a periphrastic causative; no passive; question words moved to the front.
Measured morphology: 14 live grammatical markers, mean bondedness 0.5 (0 free word … 3 fused), 5 paradigm cells, 4 of them with allomorphy.

### Grammar sketch

Built from the typology and the live markers above (planet/language/sentences.py); where the engine tracks no marker for a construction, the form is the word such markers commonly grow from, and the text says so. Examples are glossed by the Leipzig rules (abbreviations under Sample sentences).

**Number.** Nouns do not mark number: one noun form serves for one or many; a numeral or 'many' says how many.

**Case.** Nouns have no bound case. Adpositions (free words, not yet case): accusative (ACC): a separate word after the noun phrase (ʁa‼, from 'take'); ergative (ERG): a separate word after the noun phrase (je‼p, from the locative marker). Alignment is split by aspect: in the perfective or past the doer of a transitive verb takes the ergative (ERG); elsewhere the object takes the accusative (ACC).

| *w‼ɔ‼j‼* | *ʁa‼* |
| --- | --- |
| dog | ACC |

‘the dog (as object)’

| *nɛ‼ɭ-ɨnɛ‼ɭ* | *je‼p* |
| --- | --- |
| man-CL1 | ERG |

‘the man (as doer)’

**Gender and noun classes.** Nouns fall into noun classes by meaning: class 1 for a single person, a suffix (ɨnɛ‼ɭ, from 'person'); class 2 for people (plural of persons), a clitic after the noun (n‼ɪː, from 'people'); class 3 for languages, ways and tools, a separate word before the noun (kəkʰɨw, from 'tongue'); class 4 for lands, qualities and abstractions, and for every noun no other class takes, a separate word before the noun (de, from 'name').

| *nɛ‼ɭ-ɨnɛ‼ɭ* |
| --- |
| man-CL1 |

‘man’

| *de* | *o˯ɾɨw‼* |
| --- | --- |
| CL4 | day |

‘day’

**Tense and aspect.** Verbs mark tense and aspect. Past (PST): a clitic after the verb (bi‼ː, from 'yesterday'); future (FUT): a clitic after the verb (j‼ɛ, from 'go'); habitual (HAB): a separate word after the verb (laː, from 'know'). Unmarked: perfective, progressive (left to context).

| *j‼eʃiː=bi‼ː* |
| --- |
| go=PST |

‘(it) went’

| *j‼eʃiː=j‼ɛ* |
| --- |
| go=FUT |

‘(it) will go’

| *j‼eʃiː* | *laː* |
| --- | --- |
| go | HAB |

‘(it) usually goes’

**Mood and evidentiality.** Speakers mark how they know: witnessed (evidential) (DIR): a separate word after the verb phrase (uː, from 'see').

| *j‼eʃiː* | *uː* |
| --- | --- |
| go | DIR |

‘(it) goes, I saw it’

**Person agreement.** Verbs do not agree with the subject. Short unstressed pronouns stand beside the verb (2SG di‼), on their way to becoming agreement.

**Negation.** Negation is a separate word after the verb phrase (cʰɛ, from 'nothing').

| *ɔʔ* | *t̪ʰu‼=wu‼ː* | *ʁa‼* | *jɛː* | *cʰɛ* |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1SG | DEF=milk | ACC | drink | NEG |

‘I do not drink the milk.’ (sentence 6 below)

**Questions.** Yes/no questions use rising intonation alone. Question words move to the front: who ɨ, what i‼tʃʰɨj‼, where i‼tʃʰɨj‼ɨkʰ, when lu, how ʁa‼.

| *di‼* | *t̪ʰu‼=bɛ* | *ʁa‼* | *pɛ* |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 2SG | DEF=thunder | ACC | hear |

‘Do you hear the thunder?’ (sentence 4 below)

| *i‼tʃʰɨj‼* | *ʁa‼* | *t̪ʰu‼=lɨːɭ-ɨnɛ‼ɭ* | *l‼e‼ɾn* |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| what | ACC | DEF=child-CL1 | bring |

‘What does the child bring?’ (sentence 5 below)

**Commands.** There is no imperative marker: a command is the bare verb stem, with no subject and no subject or tense marker.

| *t̪ʰu‼=wep* | *ʁa‼* | *tʰaːiw* |
| --- | --- | --- |
| DEF=fish | ACC | eat |

‘Eat the fish!’ (sentence 12 below)

**Possession.** The possessor stands before the possessed noun, with no marker. Kin and body parts (inalienable) take no genitive marker. 'Having' is said with 'with' ('my mother is with a boat').

| *t̪ʰu‼=nɛ‼ɭ-ɨnɛ‼ɭ* | *w‼ɔ‼j‼* |
| --- | --- |
| DEF=man-CL1 | dog |

‘the man's dog’

| *ɔʔ* | *n‼ä-jɨnɛ‼ɭ* | *ʁi‼ɨj‼* | *ep* | *iʁɨn‼* |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1SG | mother-CL1 | boat | with | COP |

‘My mother has a boat.’ (sentence 7 below)

**Relative clauses.** Relative clause after the noun, introduced by the word for 'that' (as English that and German der grew from a pointing word).

| *t̪ʰu‼=dɛɨkʰo˯w-ɨnɛ‼ɭ* | *t̪ʰu‼kʰɨt̪ʰ* | *a* |
| --- | --- | --- |
| DEF=woman-CL1 | REL | dance |

‘the woman who dances’

**Copula.** The copula is a separate word after the verb phrase (iʁɨn‼, from 'he').

| *t̪ʰu‼kʰɨt̪ʰ* | *nɛ‼ɭ-ɨnɛ‼ɭ* | *ɛ-jɨnɛ‼ɭ* | *iʁɨn‼* |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| that | man-CL1 | merchant-CL1 | COP |

‘That man is a merchant.’ (sentence 9 below)

| *t̪ʰu‼=ji‼t̪ʰɨp* | *ə‼ɨʔ* | *iʁɨn‼* |
| --- | --- | --- |
| DEF=water | cold | COP |

‘the water is cold’

**Reduplication.** Verbs reduplicate for an action done again and again, or by many (ITER), by copying the stem's last consonant and vowel after it.

| *j‼eʃiː-ʃiː* |
| --- |
| go-ITER |

‘(an action done again and again, or by many)’

| *t̪ʰu‼=nɛ‼ɭ-ɨnɛ‼ɭ* | *t̪ʰu‼=wep* | *ʁa‼* | *jelɨleː-leː* |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| DEF=man-CL1 | DEF=fish | ACC | hit-ITER |

‘The man hits the fish again and again.’ (sentence 14 below)

**Serial verbs.** Verbs can be strung together in one clause with one subject (serial verbs): 'take X come' is 'bring'. 'Go' after a motion verb gives its direction ('run go' = run away).

| *t̪ʰu‼=nɛ‼ɭ-ɨnɛ‼ɭ* | *t̪ʰu‼=wep* | *ʁa‼* | *ʁa‼* | *ni* |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| DEF=man-CL1 | DEF=fish | ACC | take | come |

‘The man brings the fish (takes it and comes).’ (sentence 13 below)

| *si‼kʰɨʔ* | *j‼eʃiː* |
| --- | --- |
| run | go |

‘run away’

**Giving (two objects).** No dative: a serial construction, 'take the thing, give (it to) the person'.

| *t̪ʰu‼=dɛɨkʰo˯w-ɨnɛ‼ɭ* | *t̪ʰu‼=wep* | *ʁa‼* | *ʁa‼* | *t̪ʰu‼=lɨːɭ-ɨnɛ‼ɭ* | *o˯* |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| DEF=woman-CL1 | DEF=fish | ACC | take | DEF=child-CL1 | give |

‘The woman gives the child a fish.’ (sentence 11 below)

**Numerals.** Counting is restricted: a few number words, then hands and persons ('two hands' for ten), and 'many' past twenty. Twenty is nɛ‼ɭe‼j‼ə‼t and a hundred is ʁa‼n‼.

| *j‼ə‼d̪ej‼ɨnu‼ɨj‼* |
| --- |
| 6 |

‘6 = 5 + 1 ('five' and 'one')’

| *j‼ə‼d̪ej‼ɨnu‼* |
| --- |
| 11 |

‘11 = 10 + 1 ('ten' and 'one')’

| *lu‼ɨj‼ə‼nu‼* |
| --- |
| 15 |

‘15 = 10 + 5 ('ten' and 'five')’

**Linking clauses.** Complement clauses stand bare, with no complementizer.

| *t̪ʰu‼=nɛ‼ɭ-ɨnɛ‼ɭ* | *t̪ʰu‼=w‼ɔ‼j‼* | *uʁɨt̪ʰ* | *e‼l* |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| DEF=man-CL1 | DEF=dog | sleep | say |

‘The man says that the dog sleeps.’ (sentence 15 below)

**Demonstratives.** Demonstratives count two distances: 'this' pu (near) and 'that' t̪ʰu‼kʰɨt̪ʰ (far).

| *pu* | *w‼ɔ‼j‼* |
| --- | --- |
| this | dog |

‘this dog’

| *t̪ʰu‼kʰɨt̪ʰ* | *w‼ɔ‼j‼* |
| --- | --- |
| that | dog |

‘that dog’

**Comparison.** An 'exceed' comparison: 'A is big, exceeds B', with the verb for 'climb' (as Yoruba ju 'exceed', Thai kwaa 'cross over').

| *t̪ʰu‼=nɛ‼ɭ-ɨnɛ‼ɭ* | *naːw* | *iʁɨn‼* | *t̪ʰu‼=w‼ɔ‼j‼* | *pi‼ː* |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| DEF=man-CL1 | big | COP | DEF=dog | exceed |

‘The man is bigger than the dog.’ (sentence 16 below)

### Families a speaker feels

The roots a speaker still feels: a derivation or compound younger than 3 kyr whose parts are still in use (per-word `roots`). 4 families of 3+ words; 9% of the 727 words share a root with another word.

The largest: **mother** *n‼ä* (N, coined 20 kyr ago in the blue dragon proto-language); 4 words have it as their main root, 4 contain it.

### Families a historian reconstructs

The roots a historian reconstructs: every word's family as it was when the word was made, carried forward however opaque it has become since (per-word `etym_roots`, the *bher- 'carry' > burden view). 44 families of 3+ words; 44% of the 727 words share a root with another word.

The largest: **hand** *nu‼ːk* (N, coined 20 kyr ago in the blue dragon proto-language); 11 words have it as their main root, 12 contain it.

## Names of people and places

**Naming tradition.** Given names are two themes from a closed pool, compounded (as Germanic *Wil-helm*, Slavic *Vladi-mir*); the byname is the mother's name in the genitive with 'son' or 'daughter'. The tradition goes back to the blue dragon proto-language. Themes: first bear, friend, love, people, red, shine, spear, white; second fighter, heart, light, mind, peace, strong.

| **Rrirhdenï** | /r‼i‼dɛnɨ/ | 'friend-mind' | old | Rrirhdenï 'friend-mind': rrirh 'friend' + denïleew 'mind'; an old name, coined in d48 4.0 kyr ago as Rrirhdenï |
| **Dïyonrrerh** | /dɨjɔn‼r‼ɛ‼/ | 'love-strong' | old | Dïyonrrerh 'love-strong': dyonrh 'love' + rrerh 'strong'; an old name, coined in d48 4.0 kyr ago as Dyonrrerh |

| **Rrilrhïlrh** | /r‼i‼l‼ɨl‼/ | 'friend-light' | new | Rrilrhïlrh 'friend-light': rrirh 'friend' + lrhïlrhïġelrhïlrh 'light'; coined from today's words |
| **Lrhïlrhïlrhïlrh Rrirhdein** | /l‼ɨl‼ɨl‼ɨl‼ r‼i‼dein/ | 'shine-light, son of friend-mind' | matronymic | the mother's name Rrirhdenï + in 'son' (compounded: the language has no genitive marker) |

**Settlements.** **Tshanwib** /tsʰanwib/ (town, 3,395): 'the black town'; named by the gnome (d509) who founded it 4.2 kyr ago, kept as heard; **Yipupipinoġu** /jipupipinɔʁu/ (village, 1,700): 'the big fence'; named by the halfling (d381.1) who founded it 1.7 kyr ago, kept as heard; **Kubuip** /kubuip/ (village, 1,678): 'the high field'; named by the halfling (d381.1) who founded it 1.7 kyr ago, kept as heard.

## Texts

### A fable: The Bird and the Fish

One fixed short fable, told in every language as August Schleicher told his in Proto-Indo-European (1868), so that the same text shows what sound change and grammar change did. English: A bird sat in a tree. The bird saw a fish in the water. The bird said: “Come! I will give you a good seed.” The fish said: “I do not eat seeds. You will eat me.” The fish did not come. The bird ate the seed.
